items.name: design
items.prompt:
You are a motion-graphics art director studying how a top documentary YouTube channel designs its ON-SCREEN GRAPHICS. Context: Geography By Geoff, 'The Bizarre Geography of the Indian Ocean', 15:31, 1.4M views. Ignore the story; study only the visual design. Write in English, be concrete (positions as screen areas like top-left / lower third / centre, sizes as % of frame height, colours as names or hex guesses, fonts as serif / sans / condensed / handwritten, motion in plain words with rough durations). Give timestamps for every example.

1. ON-SCREEN TEXT LAYOUT: every kind of text that appears (titles, stat callouts, labels, quotes, lists, sources/credits, captions/subtitles). For each kind: where it sits, how big, font style, colour, background (none / box / blur / shadow / outline), how it animates in and out, how long it stays, how many words at once. Do they ever show 2+ text boxes stacked at once? How do they show a list of points? How do they avoid clutter?
2. TIME / ERA INDICATORS: how they show what year or how long ago a scene is (e.g. "170 million years ago", a timeline bar, a clock, chapter cards). Position, design, animation when the time jumps, and whether the narrator says the date at the same moment.
3. MAPS: map style (satellite / painted / flat colour / 3D terrain / globe), colour palette for land, water, mountains, deserts; how water is animated (rivers flowing, coastlines, sea level rising, waves); how labels are placed on maps (font, curved river labels, leader lines, pins); camera moves (zoom, pan, tilt, 3D fly-through); how they keep a map interesting while it is on screen for several seconds.
4. NUMBERS AND STATS: how a statistic (percent, distance, area, temperature) is shown and animated.
5. CHAPTER / SECTION TRANSITIONS: what happens on screen between sections.
6. THE 10 MOST REUSABLE DESIGN RULES you would copy from this video to make a geography documentary look premium and not like PowerPoint or a phone-app filter. Number them.
